9:50 PM — Act V: *Our Own Frequency* & *"Brother's Keeper"*

As the final chord of "Twin Moons: Touchdown" faded out and the Planetarium Narrator welcomed the stadium back to Earth's gravity, Evan unstrapped his bass, Tyler stepped down from the drum riser, and the twins—followed by all five members of the Orbital Crew—walked over to center stage, wrapped Ryan and Cassidy in a long, tight hug, and walked off into the stage-left wings.

The towering stadium lighting rigs dimmed all the way down until only two warm, amber living-room spotlights shone at the center of the stage deck: Cassidy seated on the bench of her gleaming black acoustic grand piano, and Ryan rolling his manual wheelchair right up flush against the left side of her piano bench—hip-to-hip and shoulder-to-shoulder—before clicking both of his wheel locks shut.

His guitar tech handed him his acoustic cedar-top dreadnought and quietly stepped offstage.

For the first time all night, there were no drum kits, no synthesizer stacks, and no hundred-watt tube amplifiers. Just a brother and a sister sitting together in the middle of a sixty-five-thousand-seat stadium as if they were back in their living room on Progress Street.

"Evan and Tyler are gonna take five backstage for a little bit," Cassidy said softly into her piano microphone, her voice carrying across a stadium so hushed you could hear the May breeze rustling the flags atop the press box. "Back in two thousand and eight, right in the middle of our ten-year hiatus, Ryan and I couldn't face the cameras or the stadiums anymore. So we locked the front door of our house right down the road on Progress Street, sat down in the living room with just an acoustic guitar, a piano, and two microphones, and recorded an album we never toured."

"We just uploaded it on a Tuesday morning with one sentence: 'We're still here, and we're okay,'" Ryan added into his boom mic, smiling out at the quiet dark. "We never thought we'd play these songs in a stadium... but tonight, sixty-five thousand of you feel just like our living room."

Sitting shoulder-to-shoulder with his sister, Ryan fingerpicked the warm, intimate acoustic intro of "Our Own Frequency" ("Just the piano and the six-string strum / Before the noise and the kingdom come / No one to tell us how the story ends / Just a brother and a sister and the time we spend / On our own frequency / Just you and me"), their voices blending in the effortless sibling harmony they had shared since they were children.

When the final acoustic harmonic faded into pin-drop silence, Ryan rested his forearm along the curve of his acoustic guitar and looked up at the sixty-five thousand people sitting in the dark around them. His heart beat a steady, honest `76 BPM` against his ribs.

"Earlier in Star City: Orbital Ward, we sang about the four-hour clock and the maintenance protocols in sci-fi metaphors," Ryan said softly, his voice echoing clearly off the quiet limestone stands. "This next song is the centerpiece of Our Own Frequency, and it's the most private song Cassidy and I have ever written—without any metaphors at all. People look up at a stage and see two hours of lights and guitars. They don't see what T-ten paralysis actually takes behind closed doors. They don't see Cassidy and Evan and Tyler helping me through my daily care and toileting routines, or stretching my legs every morning so they don't atrophy. They don't see how we push the bed against the wall at night so I can sleep on the inside, and my sister sleeps on the outside edge as a human bed rail so I don't roll off in the dark."

Across the stadium, not a single person made a sound. Down in `Section 104, Row A, Seat 1`, Ryan could see the young man in the manual wheelchair leaning forward with his hands resting on his handrims, listening intently while his friends stood close around his chair.

Beside Ryan on the piano bench, Cassidy smiled tenderly through her glasses and spoke into her mic:

"And they don't see how you keep me anchored when the world gets too loud for my head to handle. We take care of each other. That's what family does."

Ryan took a slow breath.

"Doing all of those daily routines on tour buses and in hotel rooms across the world was one thing when I was twenty-six in nineteen-ninety," Ryan continued, his voice honest and steady. "Twenty-six years later... I'm gonna be honest with you, Forger Nation. Accommodating this chair on the road has gotten too hard on my body, and on my family. Tonight is the final stop of the Reignition tour... and tonight is the last concert a touring Stardust Engine will ever play."

An audible, collective gasp rippled across sixty-five thousand people inside The Crucible, followed by a warm, deeply respectful wave of supportive applause rising from the turf.

Instantly, Cassidy leaned forward into her piano microphone, her eyes sparkling behind her glasses:

"Wait—don't be sad! We aren't retiring!" Cassidy called out over the murmur. "If touring the world is too hard on Ryan, then the world can come to Blacksburg! To give the Town of Blacksburg and CPI time to build this right, starting in August 2017, we're launching the annual Forger Nation Summer Festival! A massive CPI Open House for incoming and prospective freshmen, the biggest downtown Blacksburg block party of the summer with stages for signed and unsigned bands, and every single year we'll close the festival right here inside The Crucible with fireworks—and sleep in our own beds on Progress Street every night!"

For ten full seconds, a thunderous roar of relief and joy erupted across the stadium as the 120-foot curved LED screen behind the piano illuminated in warm gold lettering:

``` THE FORGER NATION SUMMER FESTIVAL CPI OPEN HOUSE • DOWNTOWN BLACKSBURG BLOCK PARTY • THE CRUCIBLE RESIDENCY INAUGURAL WEEKEND: AUGUST 2017 ```

As the cheers gently hushed back to pin-drop silence, Ryan whispered into his microphone, "This is 'Brother's Keeper,'" and Cassidy's fingers began the delicate, melancholy grand-piano intro of "Brother's Keeper", joined seconds later by Ryan's steady, comforting fingerpicked acoustic guitar:

> "They look at the chair and they think it's weak > They whisper their pity whenever we speak > But they don't see the mornings, the stretches and pain > The quiet routines keeping us sane > Sleeping on the edge, a human bed rail > Catching the other whenever we fail..."

One by one across the darkened stadium, sixty-five thousand fans raised quiet white phone lights into the air—not the programmed computer wristbands, just sixty-five thousand human hands holding up a warm sea of candlelight while Ryan and Cassidy harmonized on the chorus ("We trade all the armor, we trade all the scars / We built our own world underneath all the stars / When the body won't work, we become our own feet / When the pressure is heavy, we make it retreat"), flowing directly into 2008's "Safe Person".

As the final chord of "Safe Person" lingered in the quiet night air, Cassidy smiled across the piano at Ryan.

"On Reignition, we recorded the sequel to 'Safe Person' with the full stadium band," Cassidy told the crowd softly, "but since we're still sitting here in our living room with you guys, Ryan and I wanted to strip this one all the way down to just the piano and the six-string."

Without a single drum or electric amplifier, brother and sister sang the stripped-down acoustic grand-piano and fingerpicked guitar rendition of 2015's "Still Your Safe Person":

> "When the static hits a hundred and the room begins to spin > I am still your safe person—let the quiet in! > Put your headphones on or lean against my shoulder tight > I will hold the perimeter throughout the longest night!"

> *Companion Perspective (The Eleventh Child — Jordan Fuller's POV): Read Act V (`21:50–22:15`) from `Section 104, Row A, Seat 1` as Jordan listens to Ryan's speech before "Brother's Keeper" and taps `<aac>"That song is us."</aac>` in The Eleventh Child — Spring Semester 2016, Part 5: Our Own Frequency, Brother's Keeper & The Summer Festival Announcement • Explore the band's full cosmic archive at `stardust.raggiesoft.com`*.

10:15 PM — Act VI: *Saturday Night Lights* & *Progress Street*

When Evan, Tyler, and the Orbital Crew walked back out onto the stage deck at `22:15` to open *Act VI: The Homecoming Sprint***, Ryan swapped his acoustic guitar back for his sunburst electric guitar.

Because 1989's "If You Walked Away" had been permanently banned from every Stardust Engine setlist after the 1990 crash to protect Cassidy from autistic sensory and abandonment overload, they opened the full-band electric return with 1997's "Echoes in the Wire".

And the instant "Echoes in the Wire" ended, all four massive Ironstone stadium floodlight towers high above the east and west rims blazed back on at one hundred percent power—bathing the turf and the stands in the unmistakable, electric daylight of a fourth-quarter Saturday night in Blacksburg as Ryan wheeled to the front of the stage and struck a ringing stadium guitar chord.

"Back in two thousand and four," Ryan shouted into his microphone as sixty-five thousand fans leaped to their feet and roared at the sudden stadium floodlights, "we gave this next track to the university to play over the stadium speakers between the third and fourth quarters! We made a promise twelve years ago that we would never play this song live at a concert unless we were standing right here inside The Crucible! Blacksburg—welcome to the fourth quarter!"

"Hold those four fingers up, Forger Nation!" Cassidy shouted, raising four fingers toward the night sky. "Let's light up the mountains!"

The entire stadium turned into a fourth-quarter pep rally for the live concert debut of "Saturday Night Lights: The Crucible" as sixty-five thousand people jumped in unison (`"GO FORGERS! GO CPI!"`), rolling straight into "Progress Street: Where the Fire Began".

10:24 PM — *"Neon on the Huckleberry Trail"* (*"Huckleberry Trail"*)

As the final chord of "Progress Street" rang out, Marcus Vance handed Ryan his shimmering twelve-string electric guitar.

Ryan looked over at Cassidy at center stage and gave her a quiet nod. Neither of them said a word into their microphones. They didn't introduce the song, and they didn't explain it.

Instead, Ryan simply struck the opening chorused twelve-string arpeggio of "Neon on the Huckleberry Trail"—known to locals and Forgers simply as "Huckleberry Trail"—and Cassidy's warm analog synth bells chimed in at `124 BPM`.

From center stage, Ryan watched an unforgettable reaction ripple across The Crucible.

For the first two bars, all sixty-five thousand people in the stadium were in stunned disbelief that The Stardust Engine was playing something so hyperlocal at a live stadium concert without even announcing it. Right down at the front terrace railing of `Section 104, Row A`, Ryan could see students and alumni grabbing their partners' arms with wide eyes, mouthing the exact same words that scattered pockets of CPI alumni had shouted in arenas across the country: "Wait—no way! Are they seriously playing 'Huckleberry Trail' right now?!"

When they had put "Neon on the Huckleberry Trail" on Reignition the year before, Ryan and Cassidy had written it as a quiet, unassuming thank-you note to their neighbors for letting them have ten years of peace on the six-mile paved rail-trail between the Pendleton Library lawn and Christiansburg. All across the Reignition Tour—in Chicago, Los Angeles, London, or Toronto—ninety-nine percent of the arena crowds had swayed and clapped politely without having any idea what a "Huckleberry Trail" was.

Inside The Crucible, the instant the initial shock of recognition passed and Evan's bassline and Tyler's drums kicked in beneath the 120-foot curved LED screen's projection of an autumn sunset over the narrow asphalt rail-trail, disbelief turned into a thunderous roar of hometown pride as sixty-five thousand people started cheering them on!

The one percent of out-of-town fans who had driven into Blacksburg just for the concert looked around their sections in bewildered amazement, wondering what on earth was going on and why an unannounced deep cut about a local bike path was suddenly shaking the concrete deck like the biggest anthem of the night—while to the sixty-five thousand Forgers and Montgomery County residents in attendance, it was HOME.

The second Cassidy sang the closing lines of the first verse—"Six miles of asphalt from the library lawn / Where the old Huckleberry train used to roll on"—a massive, emotional cheer surged up not only from the twenty-year-old undergrads in The Anvil, who jogged and biked that paved six-mile trail past the cattle pastures and Price Mountain every afternoon, but from the lifelong New River Valley families in the lower bowl—including eighty-year-old *Walter "Santa Walt" Pendleton (`CPI Class of 1956`), the locally famous real-bearded New River Valley Mall Santa standing right at the `Section 104, Row A` railing in his maroon flat cap and cream `1956` cardigan, wiping joyful tears from his cheek with his handkerchief as he remembered riding the actual Huckleberry Train* between Christiansburg's Cambria Depot and Blacksburg before its final whistle in 1958.

By the time the second pre-chorus built toward the drum fill, something happened that nobody on stage had planned or rehearsed.

During soundcheck that afternoon, Ryan, Cassidy, Evan, and Tyler had simply expected to play "Neon on the Huckleberry Trail" straight through as a warm, breezy album track between "Progress Street" and "Neon Hearts". They had never planned a crowd singalong break for a deep cut, and there was no cue on the monitor script.

Instead, the audience made the decision for them.

Sixty-five thousand people across the lower bowl, The Anvil, and the upper decks were already singing so loudly over the pre-chorus that their voices completely overpowered the stage wedges and the in-ear monitors. Up on the drum riser, Tyler looked over at Evan with a huge, stunned grin; Cassidy stopped mid-breath with tears shining behind her glasses, realizing there was no point trying to sing over sixty-five thousand people claiming their own hometown song; and Ryan just went with the flow, leaning into his boom mic and screaming at the top of his lungs:

"Take it, Forger Nation! It's yours!"

Both of them stepped back from their microphones completely—Ryan just chiming the twelve-string chords from his wheelchair and Cassidy pressing her right hand over her heart while sixty-five thousand voices across three generations of Blacksburg and Christiansburg history carried the entire chorus across the dark valley under the shimmering autumn-gold stadium floodlight towers:

![Inside The Crucible during 'Neon on the Huckleberry Trail', a 120-foot curved LED screen projects an autumn sunset over the narrow paved Huckleberry rail-trail between wooden split-rail pasture fences while Ryan O'Connell plays his sunburst electric guitar from his manual wheelchair and Cassidy O'Connell steps back from her microphone with her hand over her heart; at the Section 104, Row A railing in the foreground, Walter 'Santa Walt' Pendleton (the locally famous real-bearded New River Valley Mall Santa and 1956 CPI alumnus in a maroon flat cap) wipes joyful tears, Jordan Fuller smiles in his wheelchair in his Foundry Maroon CPI shirt holding Aubrie Jean Kelly's hand alongside Madison Scott, Zoë Wren Brooks, and Mark Anderson, and a bewildered out-of-towner in a blue polo looks around in amazement.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/aubrie/e007/c004/p006/neon-on-the-huckleberry-trail-crucible.jpg#fullwidth)

> 65,000 FORGERS: "CHASING THE NEON ON THE HUCKLEBERRY TRAIL! > WHERE THE TWILIGHT GLOWS AND THE SHADOWS SAIL! > SPINNING OUR WHEELS THROUGH THE GOLDEN LEAVES > UNDERNEATH A SKY THAT STILL BELIEVES! > SEE THE STADIUM TOWERS FLICKER ON IN THE NIGHT > PAINTING THE VALLEY IN ELECTRIC LIGHT! > EVERY AUTUMN EVENING TELLS THE SAME OLD TALE > WE'RE HOME TOGETHER ON THE HUCKLEBERRY TRAIL!"

10:29 PM — *Neon Hearts*, *My Anchor Holds* & The False Ending

Trading their grinning sign-off ("Race you back to Progress Street!" / "You're on, Cass!") to a deafening hometown ovation, the band sprinted straight into the 1980s arena-rock punch of 1989's "Neon Hearts".

When Cassidy's warm grand piano intro opened 1987's "My Anchor Holds" under candlelight-gold and starlight-white beams, Ryan glanced out toward `Section 104, Row A, Seat 1` while playing the soaring guitar melody. There at the terrace railing, the blonde young woman stood directly behind the young man's wheelchair in his Foundry Maroon `CPI` shirt with her arms wrapped warmly around his chest and her chin resting on his shoulder, swaying with their friends as sixty-five thousand voices sang the chorus back to the stage.

Then, with Ryan's spoken grin ("Good morning, Forger Nation") and Cassidy's shout ("The switches are back on! Let's go!"), the band unleashed one more explosive burst of fireworks on the comeback anthem "Reignition: Lights Up on Progress Street" before slowing the tempo down at `22:35` for what everyone in the stadium believed was the final song of the night: 2004's "Last Bus Home: Lights Out on Progress Street".

One by one, the stage lights dimmed until only a single porch-light amber spot remained over Cassidy's piano and Ryan's chair. As the drums and bass faded to a lone upright piano chord, Cassidy leaned into her mic:

"Lights out on Progress Street..."

Ryan reached back toward the main toggle switch on his amplifier rack.

"Goodnight, Forger Nation," Ryan said softly into his microphone. "We love you."

He flipped the switch down with an audible CLICK, and every stage light, floodlight tower, and Jumbotron screen inside The Crucible cut to pitch black.

10:40 PM — Operation Anvil & The `1:40` Reveal of *"Electric Color"*

Sitting in the pitch dark at center-left stage while sixty-five thousand people cheered into the blackness—and while a few thousand fans in the upper decks began reaching under their seats for their jackets, convinced that "Lights Out on Progress Street" was the literal end of the concert—Ryan O'Connell kept his right palm resting silently over the strings of his cherry-sunburst electric guitar and listened.

Beneath the roar of the crowd, he could feel three hundred pairs of rubber-soled marching shoes moving silently up the stage-left and stage-right field ramps in total darkness.

Not a single brass player bumped a bell. Not a single snare drummer clicked a stick. Practicing the exact silent deployment they had rehearsed all semester for Operation Anvil, all three hundred members of the CPI Marching Forgers took their positions in tiered arcs across the back and wings of the stage behind Ryan, Cassidy, Evan, Tyler, and the Orbital Crew.

After ninety seconds of darkness, Cassidy pressed a single, warm, sustained chord on her grand piano.

A lone white spotlight bloomed over her at center stage. Across the stadium, people who had stepped into the aisles froze in their tracks and turned back toward the stage as Cassidy looked up at the sixty-five thousand faces rising into the Blacksburg sky:

> "Blacksburg! We've been all over the world... but there is no better feeling... > Than ending this entire tour... right here at home, in the Crucible! > Are you with us one last time Forger Nation? > Let's go!"

At `0:23`, every bank of stadium floodlights blasted on in blinding white and gold as Ryan, Cassidy, Evan, and Tyler fused with all three hundred members of the CPI Marching Forgers to unleash the towering, seventy-seven-second 1980s Album-Oriented Rock (AOR) guitar-and-300-horn brass overture that Cassidy had disguised all semester in the Marching Forgers' folders as 'Exercise 87-B: The Anvil Finale'.

It was one of the most fun seventy-seven seconds of Ryan's entire life.

Because the roaring, full-throttle 1980s stadium-rock guitar fanfare—complete with a dramatic false start, choppy tension-building syncopations, blistering twin-lead arena-rock guitars, and a three-hundred-piece collegiate brass counter-melody—sounded nothing like the glossy 1987 synth-pop radio single that Apex Records had manufactured when they stripped out Ryan's rock guitars and replaced Tyler's drums with a drum machine, nobody in the building had any idea what song they were playing. Ryan could look right out across the front rows and `Section 104, Row A` and watch sixty-five thousand die-hard fans grinning in total bewilderment—leaning over to their friends and shouting "What song is this?! Is it a brand-new song?!"

Forty seconds passed. Then sixty seconds. Then seventy-five seconds, as Ryan climbed the fretboard in a screaming dual-lead harmony with Marcus Vance and all three hundred Marching Forgers hit a colossal, stadium-shaking brass crescendo—

And at `1:40` on the dot, every guitar, synthesizer, and horn on the stage cut out completely.

In the sudden silence of the sixty-five-thousand-seat fortress, only Tyler's isolated, chest-rattling kick drum kept pounding (BOOM... BOOM... BOOM...).

Stepping up to her microphone at the front edge of the stage, Cassidy smiled out at sixty-five thousand people and sang the first four lines:

> "Woke up this morning, the world was gray > Didn't know the colors had all faded away > Been living in a room with the curtains drawn tight > Then you flipped a switch and turned on the light"

The sound of sixty-five thousand people realizing at the exact same second that they were listening to "Electric Color"—reclaimed at last as a full-throttle 1980s Stadium Rock anthem—was the single loudest human sound Ryan O'Connell had ever heard on Planet Earth.

Suddenly, even Tyler's kick drum dropped out completely, leaving Cassidy's soaring voice completely unaccompanied against the roar of sixty-five thousand people across the dark valley:

> "The city sounds were just a buzz in my ear > A static station I could never quite hear > But now the noise is turning into a song > And I finally feel like I belong"

And when the full 1980s Arena Rock band and all three hundred CPI Marching Forgers slammed in together on the chorus at maximum power, the DMX transmitters fired the final command of the night.

Across all sixty-five thousand seats of The Crucible, every LED wristband exploded into a sweeping, thirty-tier rainbow wave of electric cyan, magenta, solar gold, emerald green, and ultraviolet purple—while Ryan's overdriven electric guitar, Cassidy's soaring vocals, Evan and Tyler's thunderous rhythm section, and three hundred CPI Marching Forgers shook the Gothic limestone walls to their foundations:

> "Oh, I'm seeing in electric color > Finding a rhythm I never knew > Dancing in a brand new summer > My whole world feels bright and new > It's an electric-colored feeling > And it all started with you!"

After Evan's heavy bass groove drove through the bridge, the music cut out completely to a deafening stadium roar at `2:53`. Looking out across her alma mater, Cassidy's voice rang off the Ironstone walls:

> "Can you feel that, CPI? > That's the sound of a new world. > No more gray. > Just... color. > Here comes the solo!"

Rolling right up to the front edge of the stage at `3:07`, Ryan unleashed a massive, screaming stadium guitar solo from his wheelchair that handed off seamlessly into Cassidy's sweeping analog synthesizer solo before Cassidy called out, "Sing it with me Blacksburg! One last time!"

When the band stripped the instrumentation back down to Tyler's isolated kick drum at `4:05`, Cassidy held her microphone out toward the stands:

> "Just you! Let me hear you sing it!" > 65,000 FORGERS: "Oh-oh-oh! Electric Color!" > "I can't hear you! For the end of the tour!" > 65,000 FORGERS: "Oh-oh-oh! Electric Color!"

Looking out across the fifty-yard line toward `Section 104, Row A, Seat 1`, Ryan saw the young man in the manual wheelchair with both hands raised high into the glowing rainbow air, laughing through happy tears behind his rectangular glasses while his blonde partner and his friends linked arms around his chair.

Cassidy roared `"COME ON!"`—and the full rock band fused with all three hundred members of the CPI Marching Forgers in a colossal brass-section swell, drumline explosion, rainbow confetti cannons, and fifty-foot golden Roman candles as sixty-five thousand voices belted the final chorus into the Appalachian night:

> 65,000 FORGERS: "OH, I'M SEEING IN ELECTRIC COLOR > FINDING A RHYTHM I NEVER KNEW > DANCING IN A BRAND NEW SUMMER > MY WHOLE WORLD FEELS BRIGHT AND NEW > IT'S AN ELECTRIC-COLORED FEELING > AND IT ALL STARTED WITH YOU!"

Yeah, Ryan thought, hitting the final sustained stadium power chord alongside three hundred blaring horns and a heavy gong strike. That's why we never gave up.

As the five-minute-and-twenty-six-second chord echoed across the valley under a sky full of maroon, orange, and rainbow fireworks, Cassidy's voice rang out over the cheering stadium one final time:

> "Thank you Forger Nation! Thank you Blacksburg! > We love you! We're home! Goodnight!"

11:15 PM — The Crucible Bus Loop & Lights Out on Progress Street

When the final five-minute-and-twenty-six-second chord of "Electric Color" crashed to a halt under a sky full of maroon, orange, and rainbow fireworks, Ryan, Cassidy, Evan, and Tyler linked arms with Dr. Arthur Vance, Sarah Jenkins, and the Orbital Crew at the front lip of the stage for one final bow before sixty-five thousand screaming alumni and students.

Rolling down the stage-left hydraulic ramp into the South End Zone tunnel two minutes later, Ryan barely had time to set his brake before Holly threw both arms around his neck—her immaculate maroon blazer covered in rainbow mylar confetti and her eyes shining with tears.

"Zero leaks, three hundred thousand dollars wired to the student escrow at midnight, and the best three hours of music you four have ever played in your lives," Holly whispered fiercely against his cheek before hugging Cassidy, Evan, and Tyler. "Welcome home, Class of '89."

Thirty minutes later, after Ryan had changed into a dry maroon CPI hoodie and Evan had secured their guitars in the rear acoustic lounge of the family's 2015 Prairie Coachworks RLFD30—the thirty-foot Restyled Low-Floor executive shuttle coach they had purchased in 2015 to succeed their beloved 2004 Launch Customer `#001` shuttle immortalized on the album cover of Progress Street—Tyler took the CDL driver's seat, released the air brakes, and eased the coach quietly out of the South End Zone service gate onto Beamer Way.

With its amber LED destination sign dimmed to `OUT OF SERVICE // PROGRESS STREET` and its Obsidian Midnight and Cosmic Nebula livery blending into the night, the thirty-foot low-floor coach paused at the crosswalk beside the Crucible Bus Loop. From his locked wheelchair securement bay behind the front passenger window, Ryan looked out at the fleet of white-and-maroon sixty-foot articulated Blue Ridge Transit buses—built by the very same Prairie Coachworks factory in Winnipeg—staged nose-to-tail along the curb, their amber LED destination signs flashing `CBURG TRANS CTR` and `GO FORGERS!` in alternating letters.

Right at the front bay of the lead articulated shuttle, under the warm amber streetlamps, Ryan spotted the same young man in the manual wheelchair from `Section 104, Row A, Seat 1`—laughing with the transit supervisor in the high-visibility vest before smoothly spinning his chair 180 degrees and backing up the low-floor front ramp in reverse with two effortless, confident pulls on his handrims, followed closely by his blonde partner and his three friends.

"Hey, Cass," Ryan said softly, touching his sister's arm in the forward lounge seat beside his wheelchair bay and nodding toward the bus window. "Look who's on the lead shuttle. That's the kid from `Section 104, Row A`—the one we passed on the Huckleberry Trail."

Cassidy smiled warmly as the sixty-foot articulated bus knelt, retracted its front ramp, and pulled smoothly out into the night. "Look at that reverse ramp climb. He handles his chair almost as well as you do, big brother."

"I never did get his name," Ryan mused, watching the amber taillights of the Blue Ridge Transit shuttle turn out of the loop. "One of these days, I'd really like to meet him. Just to sit down and talk with another wheelchair user around here."

Six minutes later, Tyler turned the thirty-foot Prairie Coachworks shuttle onto the quiet, tree-lined pavement of Progress Street NE, pulled alongside the curb in front of the house they had refused `$150,000,000` to leave, and knelt the front air suspension with a gentle hiss—deploying the front-door flip-out aluminum ADA ramp directly onto their own sidewalk in five seconds flat.

There was no tour bus waiting at the curb to haul them to another city at two in the morning. There was no airport tarmac, no strange hotel bathroom, and no alarm clock set for a soundcheck five hundred miles away.

By `23:45`, after completing his final midnight Protocol T-10 check and stretching his legs with Cassidy and the twins, Ryan transferred onto the inside half of the wide mattress pushed flush against the bedroom wall.

Cassidy clicked off the bedside lamp, climbed onto the outside edge of the mattress—taking her lifelong post as her brother's human bed-rail—and reached across the quilt to rest her hand over his.

"Goodnight, Ry," she whispered in the dark.

Listening to the crickets outside the open bedroom window on Progress Street, Ryan closed his eyes and smiled.

"Goodnight, Cass. We're home."

Sunday, May 22, 2016 • 2:00 PM — The Morning After *Live at the Crucible*

On any other world tour between 1987 and 2005, the Sunday afternoon after athree-hour stadium show meant waking up stiff and exhausted in a hotel bed four hundred miles away, transferring onto a cold shower bench in an unfamiliar bathroom, and spending four hours on an interstate highway before the next arena load-in.

On Sunday, May 22, 2016, Ryan O'Connell woke up in his own bed on Progress Street NE to the smell of Evan making buttermilk pancakes in the kitchen and the sound of Blacksburg songbirds outside the window.

Even so, playing thirty-four songs across three hours from a manual wheelchair the night before had left every muscle in Ryan’s triceps, shoulders, latissimus dorsi, and lower back aching with deep post-concert fatigue.

"Come on, big brother," Cassidy said at `13:30`, holding up five swim bags with their blue plastic `$30.00/month` Town of Christiansburg Non-Resident barcode keytags clipped to the zippers. "You gave sixty-five thousand people everything in your tank last night. Today belongs to The Cove."

At `14:00`, after scanning their five non-resident keytags at the front counter of the Blue Ridge Regional Aquatic Center off Mill Lane NE in Christiansburg and changing in the private accessible Family Changing Suites, Ryan transferred out of his matte-black titanium everyday wheelchair onto one of the facility’s white waterproof PVC transfer chairs.

As Cassidy pushed his waterproof transfer chair through the glass doors into the warm, humid alcove of The Cove—the facility’s `95.5°F` warm-water therapy pool—Ryan noticed another dry custom titanium manual wheelchair (`a fourteen-pound Vanguard AeroLite-Ti` with a small brushed-silver nameplate on the crossbar reading `SHUTTLECRAFT GALILEO`) parked neatly against the tiled wall right next to where Evan parked Ryan’s dry titanium chair.

And down in the steaming `95.5°F` water along the north hydrotherapy bench, surrounded by a close-knit group of college friends, was the exact young man from `Section 104, Row A, Seat 1`—and from `5:30 PM` on the Huckleberry Trail back in October 2014.

With his rectangular polycarbonate glasses held in place by a black neoprene sport strap, the young man was floating weightlessly in the `95.5°F` water while two young women—the blonde woman who had held him during "My Anchor Holds" last night (Aubrie Jean) and their tall blonde friend (Madison)—gently supported his hips and shoulders in the warm buoyancy, slowly guiding his legs through a careful series of range-of-motion stretches to ease his post-concert muscle tone.

Ryan didn't say a word at first. Rolling down the zero-depth ramp into the `95.5°F` water, he let Cassidy, Evan, Tyler, and Holly ease him off the PVC transfer chair and spend ten quiet minutes stretching his own legs and working the three-hour guitar-strap knots out of his shoulders in the warm hydrotherapy jets.

Watching the two groups across the thirty-foot therapy pool, Ryan felt a quiet pull in his chest.

From the outside, people always assumed that being a famous rock star meant you could talk to anyone in the world. In truth, fame was deeply isolating, and living in a wheelchair inside fame was doubly isolating. For twenty-six years since the December 10, 1990 crash on Interstate 81 had left him with a complete T10 spinal cord injury, almost everyone Ryan met outside his own family fell into one of two exhausting categories: fans and industry executives who either wanted something from him or walked on eggshells around his chair, or doctors and physical therapists who interacted with him clinically. Almost never did Ryan get to simply talk to another regular guy in a manual wheelchair in his own town—someone who didn't want an autograph or a favor, and who understood the unspoken daily reality of life on wheels in Blacksburg without a single word of explanation.

Here, thirty feet away in `95.5°F` municipal water, were two families doing the exact same unglamorous, loving physical work so two manual wheelchair users could live without pain.

2:25 PM — Roommate Fluency

Once Cassidy and Evan finished stretching his legs and Ryan was floating comfortably along the submerged stainless-steel handrail, Ryan looked across the warm water and caught the young man’s eye.

Ryan drifted smoothly along the handrail until he was six feet away, with Cassidy, Holly, Evan, and Tyler floating right behind him.

"Hey, man—sorry to interrupt your stretch," Ryan said politely in a low, conversational voice, speaking directly to the young man. "Were you sitting right in the front row of `Section 104` at The Crucible last night... and wait a second, were you the guy in the manual chair who waved to us on the Huckleberry Trail back in October at five-thirty?"

Behind his water-spotted glasses, the young man’s eyes went wide with pure, unguarded shock—the unmistakable look of a college student who had been watching Ryan command a sixty-five-thousand-seat stadium less than eighteen hours ago and couldn't quite believe that Ryan O'Connell was floating in a municipal therapy pool in Christiansburg asking to get to know him.

Ryan noticed the young man’s mouth open slightly, saw the involuntary tension catch in his jaw and throat, and saw his eyes dart helplessly toward the dry changing-room corridor—unable to speak a word out loud and suddenly unsure what to do.

Before a single second of embarrassment could settle over him, the blonde woman at his left shoulder (Aubrie Jean) and the tall blonde woman at his right (Madison) moved with a quiet, practiced grace that Ryan recognized in his bones.

Feeling two quick taps of the young man’s fingers against her underwater forearm and checking his eyes first for permission, the blonde woman smiled warmly at Ryan and Cassidy.

"He’s saying a huge yes to both," she said gently. "This is my fiancé, Jordan. I'm Aubrie Jean, this is Madison—the three of us have been roommates in Bennett Hall since freshman year—and these are our family, Mark, Zoë, Lauren, Hannah, Sarah, Jessica, and Isabel. Jordan’s cerebral palsy makes speaking out loud really tough, so he uses an AAC tablet for his voice, and we had to lock it in the dry locker so the pool water wouldn't fry the electronics."

Beside Ryan in the warm water, Cassidy let out a soft, deeply moved breath, her eyes shining behind her fogged lenses. For thirty years, whenever autistic sensory overload or a crowded press room made Cassidy’s own words lock up in her throat, Ryan had stood at her shoulder and done the exact same thing Aubrie Jean and Madison were doing for Jordan right now.

"You never have to apologize for that around us, Jordan," Ryan said immediately, reaching his right hand across the surface of the `95.5°F` water. "I'm Ryan, these are my sisters Cass and Holly, and our twin cousins Evan and Tyler. It is really, really good to finally meet you, man. Just point, nod, or let Aubrie Jean and Madison translate—we speak roommate fluently in this family."

The tension melted right out of Jordan’s shoulders. Smiling from ear to ear, Jordan shook Ryan’s hand firmly—and then lifted his right hand out of the water and tapped two fingers to his temple in the exact fellow-wheelchair-user salute he had given Ryan on the Huckleberry Trail in October 2014, before tapping his chest and making a series of expressive hand gestures toward Mark and the trail.

Without missing a beat, Madison watched Jordan’s hands and eyes and translated with a warm grin, glancing at Jordan as he nodded eagerly:

"He’s saying that back in October 2014 when we passed you guys on the Huckleberry Trail, he had zero clue who The Stardust Engine was! He grew up in a house where he wasn't allowed to listen to music, so when Mark whispered your names on the trail, it meant nothing to him—he was just happy to see another guy in a manual chair out on the path!"

"And now he’s tapping my arm to add the second part," Aubrie Jean laughed softly, reading Jordan’s quick hand sign. "Three months after that walk on the trail, in January 2015, Zoë’s dad Daniel put the 1987 vinyl LP of Electric Color on his turntable in Christiansburg—and the second Daniel said your names, Jordan realized you were the siblings and cousins from the Huckleberry Trail!"

Ryan threw his head back and laughed out loud, splashing the warm water with his palm while Evan, Tyler, and Holly grinned from ear to ear.

"Are you serious?!" Ryan said, looking at Jordan with a huge grin. "Man, you have no idea how much I love hearing that! Because I'll tell you a secret, Jordan: that October evening at five-thirty when you and your friends walked past us in your CPI hoodies by the cattle pastures? When you looked over at my chair and just gave me a regular neighbor's wave without anybody pulling out a camera or treating us like a circus act—that exact moment was why Cass stopped us under the maple tree five minutes later and sang the opening lines of 'Neon on the Huckleberry Trail'!"

Jordan’s eyes went wide behind his glasses, pointing a finger at himself and his friends in amazement.

"You guys!" Cassidy beamed, nodding enthusiastically beside Ryan. "When I sang 'October five-thirty and the air turns crisp' and 'Students in their hoodies jogging two by two / Nodding with a smile as we roll on through / No autographs asked, just a neighbor's wave'—that was literally you and your family! That’s why Ryan recognized you on the camera monitor in `Section 104, Row A` before the show last night!"

For the next twenty minutes in the `95.5°F` water of The Cove, Ryan got the exact conversation he had wished for when he watched the Blue Ridge Transit shuttle pull away from the Crucible Bus Loop the night before.

He didn't have to be a rock star, and Jordan didn't have to be a fan. Floating in the warm municipal therapy pool on their `$30.00/month` Town of Christiansburg non-resident passes—with Aubrie Jean and Madison effortlessly interpreting Jordan’s gestures and nods—two manual wheelchair users simply talked shop:

Ryan told Jordan how impressed he and Cassidy had been watching him spin Shuttlecraft Galileo (`Vanguard AeroLite-Ti`) 180 degrees at the Crucible Bus Loop at `10:50 PM` last night and climb the steep Blue Ridge Transit articulated bus ramp in reverse in two pulls flat ("I told Cass on our shuttle home that anybody who backs up a kneeling bus ramp that clean has serious chair skills"). Jordan—through Madison and Aubrie Jean—told Ryan and Cassidy how `95.5°F` in The Cove was the only place in Montgomery County where gravity let go of his cerebral palsy spasticity after three hours in a stadium seat, and how he and Aubrie Jean were getting married on July 15 with a string quartet playing "My Anchor Holds" as their processional.

When it was time to roll back up the zero-depth ramp toward the changing suites at `15:00`, Ryan floated over and bumped his fist warmly against Jordan’s fist above the `95.5°F` water.

"Congratulations on the wedding, Jordan and Aubrie Jean," Ryan smiled. "We swim down here on Tuesdays and Thursdays whenever we're not locked in the basement studio. Next time we see you guys in The Cove or out on the Huckleberry Trail—at least now I finally know your name."

Volume 02 • Complete 4-Chapter Companion Novel

Book II: Before the Distance — The Story of John & Erin

Portrayed by Ryan and Cassidy O'Connell: the complete four-chapter narrative of fraternal twins John and Erin navigating Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute (CPI) in motorized power wheelchairs.

Before the Distance: The Story of John & Erin

Seconds Into Thunder

The dual-motor drive base of John's power wheelchair hummed in a steady, low-frequency harmony with Erin's chair beside him as they crested the final paved incline leading up from the Commonwealth Green to the Ironstone archway of Kincaid Hall.

Anyone who tried to navigate Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute in a manual chair learned the hard way within forty-eight hours of freshman orientation that Blacksburg was carved into the side of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Between the sweeping oval bowl of the Commonwealth Green, the steep Ironstone steps climbing toward Faraday Hall on the Engineering Quad, and the grades leading off campus toward Progress Street NE, torque and battery reserves were non-negotiable.

John eased his thumb off the rubberized joystick mounted on his right armrest, bringing his chair to a smooth, zero-radius halt just inside the warm atrium of Kincaid Student Center. Beside him, his fraternal twin sister Erin tapped her own joystick into neutral and reached up to adjust her round tortoiseshell glasses, her long wavy brown hair catching the warm amber glow of the hall sconces.

"Check your battery gauge," Erin said, glancing over at his armrest console. "That climb up from Faraday Hall always eats an extra bar."

"Four green LEDs out of five," John replied, adjusting his own matching tortoiseshell frames and smoothing the hem of his maroon sweater. He looked down the second-floor corridor toward the open double doors of the lounge, where a hand-lettered poster taped to the Ironstone pillar read FRIDAY NIGHT CAMPUS SPEED-DATING MIXER — 7:00 PM. "Which means I physically have more than enough range to turn around, take the elevator back down, and roll the two blocks home to Progress Street."

"Not a chance," Erin grinned, nudging the rubber bumper of her footplate lightly against the side of his caster wheel. "You promised me one hour out of the lab. Twenty tables, three minutes per round. If it's a disaster, we hit The Foundry for late-night waffle fries and call it field research."

They rolled side by side into the Second-Floor Lounge. The student activities volunteers had arranged twenty small circular tables in a wide ring around the room, leaving generous four-foot lanes between them so both John and Erin could maneuver their power chairs into the odd-numbered anchor spots without scraping a single chair leg. Erin claimed Table 1 near the windows overlooking Commonwealth Mall, while John parked at Table 4, flipping the standard wooden chair aside and locking his drive wheels into position flush against the tabletop.

At the front of the room, a sophomore wearing a CPI Student Activities polo stood behind a rolling media cart equipped with a dual-deck AudioStar CD system and two amplified PA speakers.

"Alright, everyone, welcome!" the organizer called out into a handheld microphone, tapping the grille twice. "Instead of using an obnoxious kitchen timer or a whistle to signal the end of each rotation, we're keeping things civilized tonight. Every round is timed to Track 3 on the new Progress Street CD by CPI's own The Stardust Engine—'Seconds Into Forever'. It's an eighty-five-BPM power ballad, and it runs exactly three minutes and zero seconds. When the synth pad fades out at the end of the song, you thank your partner and rotate one table to the left!"

He pressed play on the first round. Warm, sparkling synthesizer pads and clean electric guitar arpeggios floated out of the speakers:

The clock is ticking on the classroom wall But time stands still here in the hall I saw your face and the world went blurred The sweetest song that I ever heard No need to run and no need to hide I'm pulling up a chair right by your side

John let his shoulders drop an inch. The first three rotations were pleasant, polite, and entirely predictable—three minutes with a civil engineering major from Joule Hall debating bridge trusses, three minutes with an architecture student sketching on her napkin, and three minutes with a quiet girl from Roanoke who spent two of the minutes asking about the top speed of his power chair on the Commonwealth Green paths.

Across the room at Table 1, Erin caught his eye as the third round's sustained synth chord faded out. She flashed him a quick thumbs-up from her armrest.

See? her expression said. Harmless.

"Alright, folks, rotate to Round Four!" the organizer announced over the PA.

A woman in a fitted black leather jacket stepped into the open space opposite Table 4 and pulled out the wooden chair across from John's power wheelchair.

Unlike the previous three students, who had glanced nervously at their name tags or at the empty floor space where his chair was parked, she didn't look down at his drive wheels or his joystick controller. She rested her elbows on the small round table, leaned forward into his immediate field of view, and locked her dark eyes directly onto his behind his tortoiseshell glasses.

"I've been waiting three tables to get to this side of the room," she said, her voice low, smooth, and unhurried. "I'm Valerie."

"John," he said, offering a polite smile. "Wait—weren't you over by Table 9 a minute ago? That's five tables back."

"I traded numbers with two girls in line so I wouldn't have to wait," Valerie replied without missing a beat, flashing a sharp, magnetic smile that made John's pulse jump. "Everyone else in this room is making small talk about syllabus week. You've been actually listening to every person who sat down in front of you. You're rare, John."

Up at the front media cart, the student organizer was juggling a stack of sign-in clipboards with one hand while reaching blindly for the `|<<` restart button on the AudioStar CD player with the other. In his rush, his thumb missed the back button by half an inch and jammed down hard on `>>|` instead—skipping right past Track 3 and landing on Track 4, "Thunder in the Rain".

For ten seconds, a lush, cinematic analog brass-synth swell filled the lounge. Half the room assumed it was an extended intro to the ballad.

Then—CRASH.

An explosive acoustic drum fill and a blistering C-minor synthesizer stab tore through the PA speakers at 150 beats per minute, followed by a roaring, high-gain stadium guitar riff that rattled the water pitchers on the tables:

The clock on the wall is a guillotine blade Cutting down the promises we never made I see you standing there across the crowded floor Like a lighthouse burning on a midnight shore!

"Whoa, wrong track!" the organizer yelped, dropping his clipboards as papers scattered across the carpet. He fumbled with the volume knob, accidentally turning the master fader up before the remote slipped under the cart.

Across the room, students laughed and shouted over the sudden wall of stadium rock, waiting for him to fix the deck.

At Table 4, Valerie didn't flinch or look toward the speakers. Instead, she reached across the narrow tabletop and placed her hand directly over John's wrist where it rested near his joystick controller. Her palm was warm, her grip surprisingly firm.

Don't tell me to wait, don't tell me to stop I'm a runaway train and I'm blowing the top The neon signs are flashing "Danger" in red But I'd rather be living than safe and dead Hold on tight, baby, don't let go We're dancing on the edge of the volcano!

"Leave it!" Valerie laughed over the roaring chorus, her eyes shining as she leaned closer to John. "Everyone else gets a polite little three-minute lullaby. You and I get the storm. Tell me that isn't a sign."

John's heart hammered against his ribs in time with the 150-BPM kick drum. Used to being treated either as an academic study partner or as a Fragile Accommodation Request by strangers on campus, the sheer, undivided intensity of her focus felt intoxicating.

He smiled back into the spotlight of her attention.

"Yeah," John said over the thunder of the guitars. "Maybe it is."

Before the Distance: The Story of John & Erin

Before the Distance

Cold November rain slanted sideways across Commonwealth Mall, drumming against a wall of umbrellas and pooling in dark, diesel-streaked puddles along the granite curb beneath the vaulted Ironstone arch of The Keystone Bridge.

Along Commonwealth Mall, catching a bus at five o'clock on a weekday evening was an absolute logistical nightmare. Every single Blue Ridge Transit route staged bumper-to-bumper along the open curb between Kincaid Hall and Pendleton Library, their forty- and sixty-foot diesel engines idling in a deafening, exhaust-choked line while delivery vans, soaked pedestrians, and bicycles fought for every inch of wet asphalt.

Erin sat in her power wheelchair on the sidewalk just inside the dry stone shadow of The Keystone Bridge's northern arch, rigged properly for the Blacksburg storm: her contoured maroon CPI wheelchair rain cape was snapped taut over her knees and footplate to keep her seat cushion bone-dry, and her right hand was tucked inside the clear silicone joystick rain gauntlet sealed over her armrest controller so rainwater couldn't short the electronics. The twins' accessible ground-floor apartment on Progress Street NE was only two blocks away—a five-minute roll down the sidewalk—and John had promised to meet her here after his afternoon lab so they could head home together. Yet every thirty seconds, Erin's eyes flicked from the chaotic wall of glowing amber LED bus headboards lining the Commonwealth Mall curb down the long, wet concrete incline leading up from Faraday Hall and the Commonwealth Green.

It had been sixty-two days since the speed-dating mixer in Kincaid Hall.

In the first two weeks after that Friday night, Valerie had seemed like a whirlwind romance. She had walked beside John's power chair to every class at Faraday Hall, brought him coffee at Pendleton Library, and praised Erin as "the coolest twin sister on campus."

Then, week three had arrived, and the perimeter had begun closing like a vise.

First came the canceled Friday dinners on Progress Street NE—always explained away by a sudden "migraine" or an "emergency" that required John to take the Blue Ridge Transit bus south to Valerie's off-campus duplex in Christiansburg. Next came the phone calls where Valerie's voice was audible in the background, coaching John on what to say, followed by nights when John's cell phone went straight to voicemail for thirty-six hours at a stretch. When Erin had finally bumped into them outside the Kincaid Hall bookstore the previous week, Valerie had answered every single question directed at John, smiling coldly while resting both hands on the rear push-handles of John's power wheelchair as if she owned the chassis.

Erin's jaw tightened as two figures finally appeared through the mist at the bottom of the rain-slicked pedestrian walk from the Commonwealth Green.

John's power wheelchair was climbing the grade toward The Keystone Bridge at half its normal speed. Even from forty feet away, Erin could see why: Valerie was walking right beside his left wheel, one hand clamped tightly around the upright frame of his backrest while the other held a single black umbrella angled entirely over her own head—leaving cold rainwater to drip steadily off the rims of John's tortoiseshell glasses, pool in his unprotected lap, and splash dangerously across his uncovered right-hand joystick controller because Valerie hadn't even let him stop in the Faraday Hall vestibule to put on his wheelchair rain cape or his silicone joystick gauntlet.

As they rolled beneath the vaulted Ironstone arch of The Keystone Bridge beside the roaring curbside line of buses, Erin felt a cold knot twist in her stomach. Through the open window of the Kincaid Hall student lounge above them, the mid-tempo synth heartbeat and dramatic drums of "Before the Distance" drifted out into the November mist:

> "I saw the shadow falling across your face > A quiet surrender in a crowded place > You wore a mask, but the edges were frayed > Lost in the rules of a game that we played > I should have reached out, I should have stood tall > But I let the silence echo down the hall..."

John looked hollowed out. Dark, bruised shadows hung beneath his eyes. His shoulders were hunched inward over his armrests, his gaze fixed on the wet concrete three feet ahead of his front casters—a quiet surrender in a crowded place. He wore a polite, practiced smile as he looked up at Erin, but the edges of the mask were completely frayed.

"Hey, Er," John said quietly, his voice barely audible over the hiss of air brakes along the Commonwealth Mall curb.

"You're soaking wet, John," Erin said, driving her chair forward half a length so she was directly facing her brother. She pulled a dry microfiber cloth from her side pouch and held it out for his glasses. "Come on—home is two blocks away. Let's get you out of the rain and back to Progress Street so we can warm up and go over the thermodynamics packet."

Before John could reach for the cloth, Valerie stepped half a pace forward, positioning her hip right beside John's armrest controller.

"We have plans, Erin," Valerie said, her tone syrupy and sharp all at once. She took the cloth out of Erin's hand and wiped the rain off John's frames herself, as though John's own arms didn't work. "And honestly, John is completely burned out from carrying your shared study load this semester. He's not going back to Progress Street with you tonight. We only stopped by Commonwealth Mall so he could drop off your textbook before he gets on the bus with me for the weekend."

Erin didn't look at Valerie. She kept her eyes locked straight on her twin brother's face.

When Valerie mentioned getting on the bus to go to her place for the weekend, John's right hand—resting near his joystick—flinched almost imperceptibly, his knuckles turning white against the black foam pad. He didn't argue. He didn't correct her. He just looked down at his lap, reaching into his backpack with trembling fingers to pull out the heavy hardcover textbook.

In twenty years of sharing a life, John had never once flinched at the thought of going home.

He's trapped, Erin realized, the cold math locking into place in her chest. Home is two blocks away, and she's forcing him onto that bus to isolate him for the entire weekend.

At the curb directly beside them, a sixty-foot articulated Blue Ridge Transit coach hissed to a stop in the bumper-to-bumper lineup along Commonwealth Mall. Its amber overhead LED sign glowed through the sheets of rain—`1 FALLING BRANCH`—as the front pneumatic suspension kneeled toward the granite curb, the dual-leaf front boarding doors folded open, and the yellow-bordered aluminum ADA wheelchair ramp unfolded onto the wet sidewalk.

"That's our bus, John," Valerie said briskly, tapping the back of John's shoulder as she stepped toward the foot of the front-door ramp. "Put your chair in gear and roll on up. Erin has her textbook—she can walk the two blocks back to Progress Street on her own."

For three seconds, Erin sat frozen under the stone arch of The Keystone Bridge, the heavy textbook resting in her lap. Every polite social rule she had been raised with told her to nod, stay out of a couple's argument in public, and roll the two blocks back to Progress Street NE alone.

Then John looked back at her as Valerie nudged his backrest toward the open front door of the bus.

His glasses were fogged at the edges, his shoulders hunched against the freezing Blacksburg rain, his right hand limp and motionless beside his controller. In his eyes was a silent, drowning plea—a man about to be swallowed by the distance the second those steel bus doors closed behind him:

> "When the steel doors close and the platform clears > You can hear the truth grinding in the gears > Heed the warning hiding in his eyes > Before the distance leaves your soul behind > Trust the silence when he calls your name > 'Cause once it's gone, nothing stays the same..."

Not tonight, Erin thought. Logic is a cage when the danger is real—you can't code the panic, you can't fake what you feel. Whatever it costs me, I'm taking him back.

Before John's front casters could touch the bottom lip of the aluminum bus ramp, Erin pushed her joystick forward. Her dual electric motors engaged with a deep, authoritative hum. She drove straight out from beneath the bridge arch across the rain-slicked sidewalk of Commonwealth Mall, cutting across the concrete at a sharp angle and locking her brakes directly between John's footrests and the deployed front ramp of the bus.

Cold rain pelted her maroon CPI jacket and speckled the lenses of her glasses as she reached across the narrow gap between their armrests, covering John's cold, trembling right hand with her warm palm.

"Don't get on that bus, John," Erin said, her voice ringing clear and steady over the rumble of the idling diesel engine. "Come home with me instead. Progress Street is two blocks away."

Valerie's practiced, patient smile vanished. "Erin, excuse me—you are literally blocking the bus ramp. John and I are going to my place for the weekend, and the driver is waiting. Move your chair."

"I'm not talking to you," Erin said without glancing in Valerie's direction. She kept her eyes locked entirely on her twin brother's face, her fingers tightening protectively over his wrist on the armrest. "John, look at me. You don't want to get on this bus. I can see it in your eyes. Home is two blocks down the sidewalk. Turn your chair around and come home with me."

"Erin, I—" John's voice cracked, his chest rising and falling rapidly as he looked from the open doorway of the bus to his sister's rain-streaked face. "Valerie already made plans for the weekend, and if I don't get on the bus—"

"John, get on the bus right now!" Valerie snapped, her voice dropping half an octave as the honeyed veneer shattered in front of the whole queue of wet undergrads waiting along Commonwealth Mall. She clamped her manicured fingers tightly onto John's wet sleeve, trying to pull his arm toward the joystick to steer him around Erin's frame. "I am not standing out here in the rain having a scene with your sister! Drive up the ramp, now!"

"Take your hand off his sleeve," Erin said.

She didn't shout. She didn't have to. There was an immovable, bedrock certainty in her voice—the same quiet steel that had carried both of them through nineteen years of hospital corridors, physical therapy gyms, and steep mountain grades.

"John," Erin said softly, squeezing his hand at the foot of the ramp. "Remember the fourth-grade hill behind the middle school when my battery cable snapped in the sleet? You hooked your tow strap to my frame and burned out half your motor pulling both of us to the top. You don't owe anyone your disappearance. Don't let those doors close on you. Come home with me."

John looked down at Erin's hand clasped over his across their armrests. Then he looked at Valerie's white-knuckled grip twisting his jacket sleeve toward the bus ramp—and at the flash of cold, undisguised fury in Valerie's eyes now that the polite mask had slipped away.

Something inside John's chest unlocked.

"Last call for Route 1!" the bus operator called out from the driver's seat, his hand hovering over the ramp toggle switch. "Are you folks boarding or staying?"

"He's staying," Erin said.

"I'm staying," John echoed, his voice steadying for the first time in weeks.

He pulled his arm free from Valerie's grasp, gripped his joystick, and pulled it straight back. His electric motors hummed in unison with Erin's as he reversed his power wheelchair three feet away from the aluminum ramp, pivoting on the wet concrete until his wheels were aligned side-by-side with his twin sister's on the Commonwealth Mall sidewalk.

At the curb, the hydraulic pump whined. The yellow-bordered aluminum ramp folded upward into the front stepwell with a heavy metallic clank, and the dual-leaf steel doors hissed shut—sealing the bus closed while John and Erin remained together on the sidewalk.

Before the Distance: The Story of John & Erin

Sanctuary in the Storm

As the first articulated coach pulled away from the granite curb in a cloud of diesel spray, a second Blue Ridge Transit bus immediately rolled forward to take its place along the Commonwealth Mall sidewalk, its air brakes sighing as its front boarding doors hissed open.

Valerie hadn't gotten on the first bus. Instead, she stepped across the wet concrete directly into the path of the twins' power wheelchairs, her black umbrella trembling in her fist as freezing November rain lashed sideways beneath the arch of The Keystone Bridge.

"John, stop being ridiculous and get on the bus right now," Valerie demanded, pointing toward the open front door of the second coach idling at the curb. Every trace of the warm, magnetic woman from Table 4 was gone, replaced by a brittle, commanding fury. "The driver just opened the ramp. If you let your sister drag you down the street like a child instead of getting on this bus with me right now, we are done. Do you hear me? Get on the bus!"

A conditioned reflex twitched in John's shoulders—two months of trained muscle memory telling him to apologize, to appease her, to roll up that ramp just to stop the storm in her voice.

Beside him on the sidewalk, Erin didn't yield an inch.

She eased her thumb forward on her joystick, advancing her power wheelchair half a length and angling her heavy steel frame at forty-five degrees between Valerie and John's left drive wheel—establishing a physical, locked perimeter right on the Commonwealth Mall sidewalk.

"He's not getting on the bus, Valerie," Erin said, her voice steady and immovable over the drumming rain. "Home is two blocks from here. John is coming home."

"Stay out of this, Erin!" Valerie snapped, trying to sidestep Erin's front casters to reach for John's backrest handle again. "John, tell her! Get on the bus!"

Erin matched Valerie's step with a zero-latency pivot of her drive wheels, keeping her chair's frame locked squarely across Valerie's path so she couldn't get within arm's reach of John's controls. Then Erin looked over her shoulder at her brother and held out her left hand.

"John," Erin said gently, the storm howling down the avenue around them while her voice remained an island of absolute calm. "Take my hand. Two blocks down the sidewalk, and we're home."

John looked at Valerie standing beside the idling bus—demanding his obedience as the price of her affection—and then he looked at his fraternal twin sister, soaking wet in the November rain, shielding his chair with her own body and chassis.

For the first time in two months, the fog inside John's head cleared completely.

"Go catch your bus, Valerie," John said quietly.

Before pushing forward into the rain, Erin reached into her side saddlebag, pulled out her spare clear silicone joystick rain gauntlet and John's folded wheelchair rain cape from his rear pouch, wiped the water droplets off his controller housing with a dry microfiber cloth, and snapped the waterproof cover over his right armrest in ten seconds flat so his joystick wouldn't short out on the roll home.

Then John reached across the gap between their armrests and clasped Erin's hand firmly in his. Switching both controllers into low-torque wet-weather traction mode, he pushed his joystick forward inside the dry silicone hood.

Together, wheel to wheel on the wide brick-and-concrete sidewalk, John and Erin rolled out from beneath The Keystone Bridge, turning their backs on the Commonwealth Mall bus line and heading northeast toward Progress Street NE.

Behind them, Valerie's voice echoed sharply across the wet pavement for a few yards before the roar of the departing buses and the driving rain swallowed it whole. Thirty seconds later, as the twins crossed the corner onto the tree-lined sidewalk of Progress Street NE—just two blocks from Commonwealth Mall—John's flip phone began vibrating frantically inside his jacket pocket.

Bzzzt. Bzzzt. Bzzzt.

Every ten yards along the sidewalk, another text message arrived—first furious ultimatums, then wounded accusations, then sudden demands that he turn around and meet her at the next stop.

As they rolled up to the concrete front porch ramp of their ground-floor apartment on Progress Street NE, Erin kept her chair positioned on the outside edge of the sidewalk—maintaining her locked perimeter between her brother and the street until John's front tires cleared the porch threshold.

Under the dry shelter of the porch awning, Erin reached into John's side pocket, pulled out the buzzing flip phone, and held down the red power key until the little blue LCD screen went dark.

"Out of range," Erin said softly, tucking the silent phone into her pouch and unlocking the front door.

Inside, the apartment was warm and quiet, smelling of cinnamon, dry wool, and safe harbor. On the bookshelf stereo by the window, the dramatic grand piano and shimmering synthesizer pads of "Sanctuary in the Storm" played softly in the warm room:

> "You are my sanctuary in the storm > A fire here to keep me safe and warm > When the thunder rolls and the cold winds blow > I'll never let you go > We are a sanctuary in the storm..."

As the heavy deadbolt clicked shut behind them, sealing out the November gale, John let out a long, shuddering breath and rested his forehead against his sister's shoulder.

"You stood right in front of the ramp for me," John whispered, his voice thick as his eyes stung behind his wet glasses. "When she kept insisting I get on that bus... you locked the whole sidewalk down."

Erin wrapped her arms around his shoulders, her glasses bumping lightly against his temple, and held on tight.

"Always, John," Erin whispered back. "Home was only two blocks away. And the storm stays outside."

Before the Distance: The Story of John & Erin

Not Her

Spring arrived late on the plateau, trading November's sleet for warm April rain that smelled of wet Ironstone and blooming dogwoods along Commonwealth Mall.

It was nine-thirty on a Friday night outside the Kincaid Hall Auditorium, where the spring undergraduate research symposium had just let out. John guided his power wheelchair down the interior accessibility ramp toward the east colonnade, a rolled-up poster tube tucked beside his armrest and two cups of hot cider balanced in his cupholder tray. Erin had gone ahead five minutes earlier to grab her rain poncho from the coat check near the side exit.

As John rounded the Ironstone pillar at the end of the breezeway, the low murmur of the departing crowd faded behind the heavy glass doors—and a voice echoed from the recessed concrete alcove beside the service elevator.

"Come on, Erin, you don't need to wait around for your brother every Friday night," a smooth, practiced baritone was saying. "Honestly, it's a little unfair how much he leans on you. A girl as brilliant as you shouldn't have to play caretaker just because you share a birthday. Let me drive you home—we'll load your chair in the back of my SUV, grab a drink downtown, and you can finally have a night to yourself."

John stopped his chair in the shadow of the archway. Every nerve in his body went ice-cold, and then white-hot.

He knew that cadence. He knew the exact melody of "Not Her"—that easy charm, that practiced smile, the subtle poison designed to make love look like a burden and family look like a cage:

> "I see you move, I see your style > That easy charm, that practiced smile > You think you're clever, think you're slick > You've got your whole routine down to a trick > You see a quiet, gentle soul > Another prize to make you whole > But I've seen that look in someone's eyes before > And I won't let you walk through that door..."

In the recessed alcove by the elevator, Erin sat in her power wheelchair with her back flush against the Ironstone wall. Standing directly in front of her footrests was Garrett Sterling, a senior from the business school wearing a tailored charcoal coat. He had planted one polished leather boot on the base of the concrete ramp and rested his left hand on the top edge of the wall beside Erin's shoulder, effectively boxing her chair into the narrow corner so she couldn't pivot without clipping his shins.

"I told you, Garrett, I'm heading home with John," Erin said. Her voice was steady, but John knew his sister better than anyone alive—he saw the way her right thumb was tensed against her joystick, searching for a three-inch clearance that wasn't there. "Please step back from my footrests so I can turn around."

"I'm just saying, you let him keep you on a short leash," Garrett said, leaning in another inch with a slow, patronizing grin that expected compliance. "Just five minutes, Erin. Tell me why you're always running away when someone tries to—"

"She said step back."

John's voice cut across the Ironstone colonnade like a steel cable snapping under tension.

He didn't keep his chair in indoor low-speed mode. He thumbed his controller to its highest outdoor climbing gear and drove straight up the concrete incline into the alcove. The heavy front anti-tip rollers and steel footplate of his power wheelchair surged into the narrow gap between Garrett and Erin's chair, forcing Garrett to stumble backward half a pace or lose his ankles to two hundred and fifty pounds of rolling steel and battery torque.

John locked his brakes at a forty-five-degree angle directly in front of his twin sister, placing the full frame of his chair as a physical barricade between Garrett and Erin.

Garrett blinked, the slick smile vanishing into a flush of startled irritation. "Hey—watch where you're driving that thing, man. Erin and I were just having a private conversation."

"No, you weren't," John said. He didn't raise his voice, and he didn't look away. Behind the lenses of his glasses, his eyes were steady and surgical. "You were blocking her turning radius with your boot, putting your hand over her exit path, and trying to sell her the oldest lie in the book—that the people who protect her are the ones holding her back."

Garrett let out a sharp, defensive laugh, glancing toward the empty hallway. "You're paranoid, man. I was just offering your sister a ride home."

"I know exactly what you were offering," John said:

> "I know your game, I know your kind > The little traps you leave behind > You think she's weak, a fragile prey > But you're not taking her away > I've walked through fire, I've paid the cost > And I won't let another light be lost > Not her. Not today."

"I've heard that script word for word," John continued, his voice cold iron. "I know how it starts, I know how the flattery works, and I know what happens the moment the door closes. You can try that routine in a mirror, Garrett, or you can walk out of this building right now. Because you will never get within ten feet of my sister again. Not tonight. Not ever. Not her."

For three seconds, the only sound in the east colonnade was the low, twin hum of two power wheelchair converters idling in unison. Behind John's shoulder, Erin maneuvered her chair out of the corner until her wheel aligned parallel with his—a solid, two-wide phalanx of steel and shared resolve.

Garrett looked at John's unblinking stare, then at Erin's cold, steady gaze beside him. Whatever easy target he had imagined existed in this alcove was gone. Mutters of face-saving bravado died in his throat; he adjusted the lapels of his coat, turned on his heel, and walked briskly out the side exit into the rain.

The heavy glass door swung shut behind him.

For a long moment, neither twin spoke. Then Erin exhaled, reached across the gap between their armrests, and tapped the back of John's knuckles with her own.

"You nearly took his Italian leather toes off," Erin said, the corner of her mouth curving upward.

"He was standing in the ADA turning lane," John replied, the tension in his jaw finally softening as he handed her one of the warm paper cups of apple cider from his tray. "Come on, Erin. Home's only two blocks down the sidewalk."

Side by side, their electric motors humming in matched harmony, John and Erin rolled out under the Ironstone arches of the Kincaid colonnade and down the wet sidewalk from Commonwealth Mall to Progress Street NE—together, and all the way home.
